title: Siegard project standard
description: A project's own rules about how its source is arranged, authored by the project and never by this framework. Siegard ships this contract, the pass that holds code to a registry, and the checks that keep a finding answerable to one rule — it ships no rule. A stack's conventions are not a domain's, and a framework that shipped them would prescribe TypeScript to a Go project; the predecessor this comes from did exactly that and its own weakness list said so. It is a registry rather than prose because every finding a review records must cite exactly one rule by its id, and prose cannot be cited: a finding citing no rule is taste with a location attached. Three exclusions are the whole of its scope. First, **no rule here states what the system answers or who may see what** — a status, an error code, a refusal, an authorization outcome. Those are what the business decided, they live in the specification as nodes, and a rule here stating one would put the standard pass and the conformance pass in contradiction over the same line: one requiring in code what the other reports as a fact the specification does not hold. Second, **no rule carries a severity and nothing here derives a verdict** — the registry's ancestor graded every finding and fed the grade to an approval gate, which made the reviewer the gate. A finding states what it costs; a person decides what that means. Third, **no rule states an integration or architecture strategy that constrains the solution as a whole** — asynchronous messaging between contexts, a storage choice, an anti-corruption layer. Those are an Architecture Constraint's, in the specification, with `scope: system`; a rule here restating one leaves the same decision in two files with nothing holding them to agree, free to drift apart unnoticed. `elsewhere` is where a registry says so, the same way it already says where a domain fact or a severity actually lives.

standard.description: This standard's name, as the review that read it records it. One project may hold several — a backend's rules are not a frontend's — and each is named where it is used.

summary.description: One sentence saying what this standard governs, not that it is a standard.

rules.description: Every rule this standard declares, each with an identifier a finding can cite. Ids are unique across the registry: two rules under one id cannot be told apart by the finding that cites it.

presupposes.description: The artifacts this registry's rules assume already stand — the manifest whose script a rule names, the compiler configuration whose strictness a rule requires, the dependency declaration a rule forbids a second of. A rule is a condition over a file that exists and never a requirement that one does, and `applies_to` cannot say otherwise: a scope names a directory and an ending, so it reaches no artifact sitting outside a directory and nothing in a rule can ask for one at all. Stating them here is what lets a delivery refuse before it writes. A registry whose substrate is absent is a registry that cannot be applied — its tool-decided rules have no step to run as, and its read-decided rules are held against files that were written to answer nothing — and the absence then surfaces as one finding per file in a review, after the source exists, rather than once, before the first line of it. A project whose substrate already stands declares none, and a registry declaring none is held to nothing extra.

dependencies.description: The direct dependencies this registry authorizes a delivery to install. It is an allowlist, and it exists because installing is not writing: a package brings code nobody here read and runs some of that code at install time. Named here, it goes in without anybody being asked; absent, a delivery that needs it stops and names it, and the approval that ends the stop is this list gaining the package — never an answer inside a session, which the next invocation does not have. Transitive dependencies are outside it and always will be: no package manager offers a closure anybody approved, and what actually arrived is made reproducible by the lockfile the project commits, not by this list.
dependencies.$comment: Held against an implementation record's `installed` by bin/deliver.py.

commands.description: How this project is installed, checked and run, as steps a caller names to `bin/run.py`. The framework composes none of them and infers none from what it finds in a tree: a runner that guessed a test command would be answering a question about the consumer's project, and the guess would be wrong in the project that mattered. What declaring them changes is who names them. Left to a human to retype at every invocation, they were not named at all — which is how one registry reached twenty-four rules decided by a tool with no step ever run to decide any of them. A registry that declares none behaves the way every registry did before this field: nothing runs on its own, and a review says which rules went unanswered.
commands.$comment: Read by /implement-task and /review-change, and passed to bin/run.py as --step NAME=COMMAND.

elsewhere.description: What this standard deliberately does not hold, and where each of those lives instead. It is written for the reader who looks for a rule, does not find it, and would otherwise conclude nobody thought of it — the same reason a plan declares its uncovered remainder and a review declares the passes that did not run. Nothing validates the destinations, and nothing has to: this is the registry saying out loud which of the three homes a question belongs to.

slug.description: A name reduced to kebab-case. A name that will not reduce is a refusal, not a transliteration.

allOf.$comment: The reverse — a rule decided by reading naming a tool — is refused by bin/deliver.py, which can say so in a sentence a reader acts on.

id.description: How a finding cites this rule. Short and stable: an id that changes orphans every finding that cited it, and a review from last month is read beside the registry as it stands.

statement.description: What the rule requires, as one condition a reader can hold a file to. "Keep the code clean" is not a statement; "a service or controller never constructs a dependency" is.

because.description: What goes wrong when the rule is departed from, as a consequence rather than as the rule restated. It is required because a rule with no stated reason is an arbitrary constraint that nobody can weigh a departure against, and because it is the material a finding's `cost` is written from: the reviewer says what this departure costs here, in the terms this field gives.

decided_by.description: Which half of the standard this rule sits in, and this is the field that decides who applies it. `reading` means telling whether the rule holds requires understanding what the code means — a responsibility that spans two layers, an interface a caller cannot satisfy. Those are the standard pass's, and a review's findings cite them. `tool` means a linter, a compiler, a formatter or a secret scanner decides it exactly and cheaply — a forbidden construct, a name's shape, a file's length, an interpolated query. Those are not a model's work: they run as steps of the caller's own suite, their failures arrive as a captured run, and the failures pass reads what the tool printed. A model applying a rule a linter owns has strictly worse recall than the linter and costs more, and the validator refuses a standard-pass finding that cites one.

tool.description: Which step decides this rule, named as the caller names it to the runner. Required when `decided_by` is `tool`: a rule declared mechanical with nothing named to decide it is a rule nobody applies, which is worse than one nobody wrote.

applies_to.description: Where this rule reaches. A rule with no scope is a rule that fires on every file including the tests, and the finding it produces is one nobody can act on. The scope is stated in parts rather than as a glob pattern so that a validator can check a finding against it without a pattern language: what a glob means differs between tools, and the difference would decide whether a finding is refused.

seen_at.description: A path in this project where the rule is already obeyed. Optional and worth writing: a rule with an example is a rule an implementer can follow without guessing the shape, and it is the same discipline an inventory node applies to a convention — one observed at nowhere is an opinion.

under.description: The directory this scope starts at, relative to the target source root and without a trailing separator.

suffix.description: What a path must end with — an extension, or a role and an extension together such as `.service.ts`.

nested.description: Whether the scope reaches directories below `under`. Absent is false: the scope is exactly the files sitting directly in `under`. This is the distinction a glob language gets wrong in both directions — one tool's single star crosses a separator and another's double star means exactly one directory — so it is stated rather than pattern-matched.

path.description: Where the artifact sits, relative to the target source root — the directory the project's own commands are run from, which is the root a scope's `under` is stated against. Whether it exists is the whole of what a script decides here. Whether what it holds is right is decided by the project's own suite, through the steps the tool-decided rules name, because a framework that read this file would be reading a stack it ships no knowledge of.

provides.description: What the rules below get from it, in one sentence. It is the material a task's criteria are written from when the artifact has to be built, so `the manifest` says nothing worth acting on and `the test script STK-10 names and the module type STK-02 depends on` says what has to be there.

rules.description: The rules of this registry that cannot be satisfied while the artifact is absent, by identifier. Required and non-empty: a presupposition no rule needs is not this standard's to state, and naming them is what lets a refusal say what the absence costs instead of merely that something is missing. Each must be a rule this registry declares — an identifier that no longer resolves is a presupposition nobody can weigh, and `bin/deliver.py` says so.

package.description: The dependency's name, exactly as this project's package manager names it. It is the string a delivery records having installed and the string this list is checked against, so a name spelled two ways is two packages. No version is stated: a version fixed here would be a second home for what the project's lockfile already holds, and the two would disagree the first time either moved.

why.description: Why this project admitted it. Where a rule needs the package, that rule's need in a sentence; where a human approved it on its own, this is the approval — the field exists because an approval that lived in a conversation is one the next invocation does not have, and a package admitted with no stated reason is one nobody can later reconsider.

rules.description: The rules of this registry that need this package, by identifier. Optional, because a package may be admitted for a reason no rule states — that is what `why` carries — but where a rule does need it, naming the rule is what lets a reader see what removing the package would break. Each must be a rule this registry declares.

timeout_seconds.description: How long this step may take before it is terminated. Required, and stated by the project rather than shipped: a bound this framework chose would be one nobody calibrated, and an unbounded run is worse than a wrong bound because nothing ends it. `bin/run.py` takes one timeout for a whole run, so a run holding several steps is given the largest of theirs — a step that finishes in a second is not made to fail because it shares a run with an install that may take five minutes.

step.description: What this step is called, and it is the join that holds the whole split together: a rule's `tool` names it, `bin/run.py` records its outcome under it, and a review reads that outcome by it. The shape is the one the runner already requires of a step name — a name it would refuse is a step nothing can run.

command.description: The command, exactly as it is run. `bin/run.py` splits it into an argument vector and executes it directly with no shell, so nothing here expands `&&`, a pipe, a redirect, a variable or a glob; a step that needs any of those is written into a file, and that file is the command.

role.description: What this step is to a delivery, where it is more than a check. `install` is what makes the packages this registry authorizes real, and it runs before anything is written against them. `suite` is what proves the work, and it is held back until the tests exist — every other step runs on both sides of that line, which is how a rule about how tests are written gets decided at all. At most one step carries each. A step carrying neither is an ordinary check that runs with the rest. A registry may authorize packages and declare no `install`: where a project holds several registries, one of them owns the manifest and the others own the steps their own rules are decided by. What that costs is said where it is felt — an invocation handed such a registry alone has nothing to install with, and says so.

lives_in.description: Where this actually lives — the specification, a named agent of the framework, a tool, or nowhere on purpose.

examples.summary: How this service layers its modules and wires them together.

rules.statement: A constructor receives interfaces, never concrete implementations.
rules.because: A class bound to a concrete collaborator cannot be exercised without it, so a test has to stand up the collaborator's world to assert one line of this one.

rules.statement: Production code logs through the configured logger; console output is not used.
rules.because: A console line goes nowhere in production — no level, no correlation, no retention.

presupposes.provides: the `lint` step PRH-01 is decided by, and the declaration of the configured logger PRH-01 requires production code to reach.

dependencies.why: PRH-01 requires production code to log through the configured logger, and this is it.
the `lint` step PRH-01 is decided by runs it.

elsewhere.what: Which status a refusal answers with.
elsewhere.lives_in: The specification, as a rule or contract node.
elsewhere.why: It is what the business decided, and stating it here would make two review passes disagree over one line.
